newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Morocco to U.N. - don't change W.Sahara peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Morocco to U.N. - don't change W.Sahara peace plan.

text.p: Morocco has told Secretary-General Kofi Annan it objects to any changes in a U.N. peace plan for Western Sahara involving an oft-postponed referendum on the future of the former Spanish territory.

In a letter to the U.N. chief circulated on Thursday, Moroccan U.N. envoy Ahmed Snoussi said a recent report by Annan indicated he was reviewing the peace plan, including the possibility of making adjustments.

"The Kingdom of Morocco has affirmed repeatedly its attachment to full implementation of the settlement plan. It considers that the drafting of the plan was a long and arduous process and that altering it ... could prove to be an even longer and more complex process."

The U.N. plan calls for a referendum, originally scheduled for January 1992, to decide whether Western Sahara should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of the territory, or become independent as called for by the Polisario Front.

A brushfire war was largely halted by a U.N.-monitored ceasefire in September 1991. But continuing differences between the two sides over who should be allowed to vote in the referendum has caused repeated postponements and voter identification has been stalled since late 1995.
Snoussi said that, "while Morocco remains committed to the settlement plan, the other party is doing its utmost to delay the referendum process and even prevent it from taking place."

Regretting that Annan's report did not specify why the voter identification process had stalled, he said Morocco defended the "right of any person to take part in the referendum process who can prove that he or she belongs to Western Sahara," and that this coincided with the U.N. position.

Referring to Polisario, he said: "The other party is opposed to that right and has made its participation in the identification process subject to two conditions which are contrary to the spirit and letter of the settlement plan."

He said Polisario was trying to restrict the right of Saharans to participate in the referendum "by limiting that right to persons whose names appear in the Spanish census of 1974, a census whose omissions and flaws have been acknowleged by all forums."

Snoussi said Polisario also wanted the lists of those found eligible to vote by an identification commission to be made available, though the U.N. plan said that should be done only at the end of the identification process and after the lists had been approved by the secretary-general.
Annan is widely believed to be planning soon to appoint former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker as a special U.N. envoy for Western Sahara to revive efforts to find a solution.
